questions.question: A 29-year-old lady has been experiencing loss of appetite, profuse sweating, and palpitations for the past three months. Laboratory tests conclude increased T3 and T4 levels with decreased TSH levels. A representative HPE of this condition is shown below. The most common antibodies in this condition target which of the following?

explanation.text: The HPE image shows features of Grave’s disease most commonly as Long-acting thyroid stimulator antibodies that target the TSH receptor. The HPE image shows the microscopic finding of Graves disease, characterised by Follicles are lined by hyperplastic, enlarged epithelial cells that project into the lumens of the follicles, forming papillary projections. These are called Pseudopapillae (vs true papillae containing a fibrovascular core).

These cells actively resorb the colloid in the centres of the follicles, resulting in the scalloped appearance of the colloid's edges. Antibodies in Graves disease: TSI - Thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin or LATS - Long-acting thyroid stimulator. These antibodies attach to the TSH receptor and stimulate them, leading to excessive release of T3 and T4. This results in hyperthyroidism

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman comes to the office due to progressively worsening eye irritation and double vision over the last two months. She also reports unintentional weight loss, mood swings, diarrhoea, and palpitations. Physical examination shows tachycardia and bilateral proptosis. What is the pathophysiology causing proptosis?

explanation.text: This patient with hyperthyroidism (weight loss, palpitations, tachycardia) and significant ophthalmopathy (proptosis, diplopia) has Graves disease with ophthalmopathy, which is due to increased activity of orbital fibroblasts. Graves disease is an autoimmune disorder triggered by thyrotropin receptor antibodies that activate the TSH receptor. The TSH receptor is also on fibroblasts, adipocytes, and other cell types.
Triad in Graves: Hyperthyroidism Proptosis Pretibial myxoedema- infiltrative dermopathy due to thickening of the dermis due to deposition of glycosaminoglycans and lymphocyte infiltration

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the gross morphology of Riedel’s thyroiditis?

explanation.text: Riedel's Thyroiditis belongs to an IgG4-related disease that causes extensive fibrosis. Fibrosis causes the thyroid to become stony and hard. It also attaches the thyroid to the adjacent tissues, muscles, and vessels implying the mass is fixed and does not move with deglutition. So it behaves like/mimics a cancer.

Other IgG4-related diseases include: Mikulicz syndrome- Affects salivary and lacrimal gland Kuttner syndrome- Sclerosis of the submandibular gland Ormond disease- Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis Angiocentric fibrosis- Involves nasal cavity

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis?

options.B: Usually presents as a painful enlargement of the thyroid

explanation.text: Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis is typically a painless enlargement of the thyroid. Usually presents postpartum in 5% of women and is presumed to have an autoimmune aetiology. The self-limiting condition does not usually require treatment Characterised by lymphocytic inflammation in the thyroid.

questions.question: What is the finding in the histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen from a patient with De Quervain Thyroiditis?

options.A: Extensive stromal fibrosis extending beyond the thyroid capsule
options.C: Mononuclear infiltration with well-developed germinal centres
options.D: Mixed cellular infiltration with occasional multinucleated giant cells

explanation.text: Painful enlargement of the thyroid gland following a viral infection such as mumps, is suggestive of de Quervain thyroiditis. The microscopic findings include: Large multinucleated giant cells Giant cells with engulfed colloid Mixed cellular infiltration

questions.question: A 55-year-old patient presents with a solitary thyroid nodule. The patient also reports difficulty swallowing, with no complaints of weight loss, fatigue, or heat intolerance. An excisional biopsy reveals >75% of the following characteristic cells. Which genetic mutation is most commonly associated with this type of thyroid tumour?

explanation.text: The above image shows cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and small regular nuclei, suggesting Hurthle cells. The presence of >75% of these cells indicates a Hurthle cell tumour, a rare thyroid neoplasm of follicular cell origin associated with RAS mutation. Hurthle cell adenomas are variants of follicular adenoma, and the presence of more than 75% of Hurthle cells is a key diagnostic feature.

Hürthle cell (oxyphil) adenoma comprises cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and small regular nuclei. questions.question: A 40-year-old patient presents with a nodule in the anterior neck and lymphadenopathy. The tumour is found to have spread to the lymphatics. Histopathological examination shows characteristic findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The above features and HPE showing psammoma bodies, nuclear grooves, and " Orphan Annie eye" nuclei are indicative of papillary thyroid carcinoma. This is the most common type of thyroid cancer and is characterised by lymphatic spread. It often presents with a nodule in the anterior neck and lymphadenopathy. Associated with BRAF mutations and RET-PTC fusion HPE shows: True papillae- Fingerlike projections with fibrovascular core.

Orphan Annie eye nuclei - Optically clear nucleus produced due to artefact. Intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions (INCI). Nuclear groove or coffee bean nucleus. Presence of psammoma bodies- Dystrophic calcifications It has the best prognosis among thyroid malignancies Follicular thyroid carcinoma (Option A): Typically spreads haematogenously (to bone, lungs), not via lymphatics. Requires capsular and vascular invasion for diagnosis.

**Medullary thyroid carcinoma (Option B):** Arises from parafollicular (C) cells, associated with calcitonin production and sometimes MEN syndromes. Histology shows amyloid stroma, not papillary features.

**Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (Option D):** A very aggressive and undifferentiated tumour, usually in elderly, presents with rapid growth and poor prognosis. Histology shows pleomorphic, spindle cells, not papillary patterns.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a common feature of follicular carcinoma of thyroid?

options.D: FNAC is not helpful in diagnosis

explanation.text: Spread by lymphatic route is not a common feature of follicular carcinoma as they commonly spread by hematogenous route. Follicular carcinoma of thyroid is the second common malignancy of thyroid following papillary Ca. They are commonly associated with K-RAS mutation Capsular and vascular invasion on biopsy is a diagnostic feature of follicular carcinoma. FNAC is not helpful in diagnosis of follicular carcinomas.
Regional lymph nodes are typically not involved and hematogenous spread to bone, lungs and liver are more common.

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with a painless lump on the front of the neck, bone pain, fatigue, and episodes of flushed skin. Genetic studies reveal a mutation in the RET gene. Which type of amyloid is typically deposited in this condition?

explanation.text: The given scenario and mutation are associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma, which has amyloid deposition derived from calcitonin, known as A-CAL. Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid is a neuroendocrine tumour arising from parafollicular C cells. They secrete calcitonin, which regulates calcium levels and is also a marker for diagnosis and postoperative follow-up. Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a marker in which calcitonin is negative.

They can be sporadic or associated with familial syndromes like MEN 2. Both have associated RET mutations. Sporadic tumours usually present with solitary nodules whereas familial ones are characterised by bilaterality and multicentricity, and can have features of other associated tumours. A biopsy would show amyloid deposits (Acal) derived from calcitonin polypeptides.
A-β ( Option A): It is associated with Alzheimer's disease.
**A-L (Option C):** Is associated with primary amyloidosis and multiple myeloma, derived from immunoglobulin light chains.
A-TTR ( Option D): It is associated with transthyretin and is seen in conditions like familial amyloid polyneuropathy and senile systemic amyloidosis.

questions.question: Which of the following cell types are typically found in the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland, and which are stained pink and purple, respectively?

explanation.text: The scenario suggests acidophils and basophils seen in the anterior pituitary. Lactotrophs and thyrotrophs are examples of cells found respectively with these staining. The pituitary consists of 2 lobes. Anterior pituitary/ Adenohypophysis - Contains many hormone-producing cells. These cells can be acidophilic, basophilic or poorly staining based on the staining pattern.

Acidophils- Eosinophilic/pink colored- Sommatotrophs and lactotrophs Basophils- Basophilic/blue colored- Corticotrophs, thyrotrophs, and gonadotrophs Chromophobe cells- poorly staining cytoplasm 2. Posterior Pituitary/Neurohypophysis- Contains nerve endings from the hypothalamus that store and release hormones produced in the hypothalamus.

questions.question: Pituitary adenomas are often classified based on the hormones they secrete. Which of the following statements correctly matches the type of pituitary adenoma with its primary hormone secretion and associated syndrome?

options.A: Prolactinoma – Secretes prolactin – Causes Cushing's disease
options.B: Somatotroph adenoma – Secretes growth hormone – Causes acromegaly
options.C: Corticotroph adenoma – Secretes thyroid-stimulating hormone – Causes hyperthyroidism
options.D: Gonadotroph adenoma – Secretes adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) – Causes Addison's disease

explanation.text: Adenoma type Hormone secreted Associated condition Prolactinoma Prolactin Hyperprolactinemia Somatotroph Adenoma Growth Hormone Gigantism (Children), Acromegaly (Adults) Corticotroph Adenoma Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) Cushings disease Gonadotroph Adenoma Gonadotropins (LH and FSH) Often asymptomatic, may cause hypogonadism A) Prolactinoma secretes prolactin, leading to hyperprolactinemia, not Cushing's disease.

B) Somatotroph adenoma secretes growth hormone, causing gigantism in children and acromegaly in adults. C) Corticotroph adenoma secretes adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which leads to Cushing's disease, not thyroid-stimulating hormone or hyperthyroidism. D) Gonadotroph adenoma secretes gonadotropins (LH and FSH) and is not associated with ACTH or Addison's disease.

questions.question: A pathologist examines a surgically resected pituitary tumour under a microscope. The tumour comprises sheets of monomorphic, round to polygonal cells with central nuclei and sparse to absent reticulin network. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: Pituitary adenoma: Pituitary adenomas are benign tumors that arise from the pituitary gland and are characterized by sheets of monomorphic, round to polygonal cells with central nuclei and a sparse to absent reticulin network Cellular monomorphism and the absence of a significant reticulin network distinguish pituitary adenomas from normal anterior pituitary parenchyma. •They are well-circumscribed and encapsulated. •They are the most common type of pituitary tumor and can be classified based on size as follows.
Pituitary carcinoma ( Option B): Is very rare and have malignant cells showing nuclear pleomorphism along with invasive growth and metastasis.

**Schwannoma (Option D):** Schwannomas are tumors of Schwann cells found along peripheral nerves. They display spindle-shaped cells in a palisading pattern and stain positive for S-100 protein. They do not arise in the pituitary gland.
**Craniopharyngioma (Option C):** Incorrect – Shows squamous epithelium, calcification, and wet keratin, not monomorphic sheets or reticulin loss.

questions.question: A 12-year-old child presents with headaches, visual disturbances, and delayed growth. An MRI of the brain reveals a 3 cm cystic mass with calcifications. The growth was found to be encapsulated and multiloculated. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: Craniopharyngioma: Craniopharyngiomas are benign tumours arising from vestigial remnants of the Rathke pouch They commonly occur in the suprasellar region and often present as encapsulated and multiloculated cystic masses with calcifications. The cysts contain cholesterol-rich, thick brownish-yellow fluid (compared to machine oi)l It has 2 histological variants: Adamantinomatous and papillary.

Feature Adamantinomatous Papillary Age group Children Adults Epithelium Stratified squamous Stratified squamous Wet keratin + - Calcifications + - Cysts + - Stellate reticulum + - Common presentations include headaches and visual disturbances like bitemporal hemianopia due to optic chiasma compression, while children present with growth retardation due to pituitary hypofunction and GH deficiency.

**Oligodendroglioma (Option A):** Typically affects adults (30–50 years old). Commonly located in cerebral hemispheres, not suprasellar. Calcifications can be present, but they are intra-axial and not cystic or multiloculated. Endocrine symptoms are rare.

**Age and symptom mismatch Meningioma (Option B):** Rare in children; typically seen in middle-aged to older adults. Usually extra-axial, solid, may calcify but are not cystic or multiloculated. Often incidentally found unless very large. Does not cause hormonal dysfunction in children.

**Age and imaging mismatch Pituitary Adenoma(Option D):** Unlikely in a child.Pituitary adenomas are rare in children. Typically cause endocrine symptoms, but visual changes in children from adenomas are uncommon. Less likely to be calcified or multiloculated. Usually solid tumors, not cystic. Age, imaging, and morphology mismatch

questions.question: A 35-year-old male presents with a history of recurrent kidney stones, hypercalcemia, and a recent diagnosis of a pituitary adenoma. Which of the following syndromes is most likely associated with his clinical presentation?

explanation.text: The given clinical scenario of hypercalcemia and radiological finding of pituitary adenoma is suggestive of MEN1 Genetics: Autosomal dominant; MEN1 mutation on chromosome 11q13. Common Tumors: Anterior Pituitary: Prolactinoma. Parathyroid Adenoma: Most common. Pancreatic Tumors: Gastrinoma (MC, often in the duodenum). Other Associations: Angiofibroma, collagenoma, lipoma, meningioma, VIPoma, foregut carcinoid.

Clinical features often include primary hyperparathyroidism (leading to hypercalcemia and recurrent kidney stones), pituitary adenomas, hypoglycemia due to insulinomas, and peptic ulcers in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
**MEN 2A syndrome (Option A):** Associated with mutations in the RET proto-oncogene. Clinical features include medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytomas, and parathyroid hyperplasia.

**MEN 2B syndrome (Option B):** Also associated with mutations in the RET proto-oncogene. Clinical features include medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytomas, mucosal neuromas, and Marfanoid habitus.
**MEN 4 syndrome (Option D):** Caused by mutations in the CDKN1B gene. Similar to MEN 1 but can include additional features such as tumors of adrenal, kidneys, and reproductive organs.

questions.question: Which mutation is associated with pituitary carcinoma?

explanation.text: Pituitary adenoma treated with surgery, radiation therapy, and subsequent symptoms that include adjacent structure invasion point to a diagnosis of pituitary carcinoma which has HRAS mutation. HRAS mutation is a somatic activating mutation affecting mitogenic signaling cell growth and survival.

questions.question: Identify the marked cells in the histology of the parathyroid below.

explanation.text: The marked cells with light pink cytoplasm and centrally placed nuclei in the histology of the parathyroid gland are called chief cells.
**Oxyphil cells (Option A):** are dark pink, and have eosinophilic granular cytoplasm.
**Adipocytes (Option C):** are fat cells with clear cytoplasm due to the dissolution of fat content during tissue processing.
**Parafollicular cells (Option D):** are seen in the thyroid gland, interspersed between thyroid follicles, and stain pale.

questions.question: Which of the following microscopic features is most indicative of a parathyroid adenoma rather than parathyroid hyperplasia?

options.A: Diffuse hyperplasia of chief cells throughout the parathyroid gland
options.B: Stromal fat infiltration within the parathyroid tissue
options.C: Intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions within chief cells

explanation.text: Parathyroid adenoma and parathyroid hyperplasia are microscopically identical and difficult to differentiate. All microscopic features mentioned are seen in both parathyroid adenoma and parathyroid hyperplasia.

Diffuse hyperplasia of chief cells throughout the parathyroid gland Stromal fat infiltration within the parathyroid tissue Intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions within chief cells Grossly, parathyroid adenoma occurs as a distinct nodule within a capsule and parathyroid hyperplasia classically affects all four glands. Syndromes associated with parathyroid adenomas: MEN-1 MEN-2 MEN-4 Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (rare)
